strengths: Clear problem framing via three well-motivated desiderata (D1-D3) with a systematic comparison table against representative prior work (Max Loss, Max Grad, RHO-Loss, GREATS).

Novel and efficient signal design: reusing forward-pass logits (nuclear norm) for utility/intra-sample diversity avoids extra backprop, and a Kronecker-factorized SRFT-style projection (Theorem 3.2) provides a theoretically grounded, storage-efficient way to compute inter-sample diversity via a memory buffer, with complexity reduced from O(NVd) to O((N+V)d log(NV)).

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation across two backbones (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B) and four diverse benchmarks (MMLU, ScienceQA, GSM8K, HumanEval), with consistent accuracy gains over strong baselines (GREATS, RHO-Loss) and higher throughput than several competitors.

Good supplementary analysis: ablations isolating the nuclear-norm-only and diversity-only components, sensitivity studies on projected dimension d1/d2, memory buffer size M, and trade-off factor α, plus an empirical loss-reduction vs. nuclear-norm correlation plot (Figure 2) supporting the utility claim.
Reasonably reproducible: hyperparameters, dataset statistics, and training configurations are reported in detail in the appendix.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification linking nuclear norm to 'optimization utility' relies on a first-order Taylor approximation and an informal claim that the label-probability gradient term Δ is 'less sensitive to scale' than the logits perturbation; this is not rigorously established and is validated only with a single correlation plot (Qwen-2.5-7B on MMLU), leaving the generality of the claim across models/datasets unverified.

The intra-sample diversity argument (low-rank logits => repetitive predictions, high-rank => diverse/informative predictions) conflates prediction confidence/calibration with lexical diversity; a confidently correct deterministic sequence could also yield varying row directions, and the paper does not empirically disentangle scale (Frobenius norm growth) from rank/diversity effects, despite claiming both are captured.

Key hyperparameters (data selection ratio K per dataset/model in Table 5, and the trade-off factor α in Table 6) appear to be tuned per benchmark/backbone combination with fairly narrow optimal ranges (per Figure 7's inverted-U shape); it is unclear how these are selected in practice without access to held-out validation performance, which seems to implicitly conflict with the stated D2 desideratum of avoiding external resources/validation sets.

Experiments are conducted only with LoRA (rank=8) rather than full fine-tuning, which is the more common and computationally expensive regime where online batch selection would matter most; it is unclear whether the method's benefits and efficiency claims transfer to full-parameter SFT.

Ablation studies (Table 4) and sensitivity analyses are performed only on Qwen-2.5-7B, not on Llama-3.1-8B, limiting confidence that the two-component design and hyperparameter trends generalize across backbones.

No comparison to offline data-selection SOTA baselines (e.g., LESS, Alpagasus) discussed extensively in the related work section, despite these being natural competitors under a similar data budget; only online selection baselines are compared.

The magnitude of improvement is uneven and occasionally very large (e.g., +5.15% over GREATS on MMLU with Qwen at a low 12.5% selection ratio) compared to more modest gains on other benchmarks, without deeper analysis of why some settings benefit disproportionately, raising questions about robustness of the reported gains.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated, with a clear articulation of three desiderata (D1-D3) that expose real gaps in prior online batch selection methods (utility-only heuristics, external-resource dependence, computational overhead), and Table 1 gives a clean comparative framing.

The core idea of using the nuclear norm of the logits matrix as a joint proxy for optimization utility and intra-sample diversity is a genuinely interesting and relatively novel connection; it is supported by a first-order Taylor-expansion argument (Eqs. 5-8) plus an empirical Spearman correlation study (Figure 2) linking nuclear norm to actual loss reduction.

The low-dimensional projection for inter-sample diversity is technically solid: reducing the storage of a naive O(NV x d) projection matrix via Kronecker-factored Γ1, Γ2 is shown (Theorem 3.2, Appendix C.3) to reduce exactly to a subsampled randomized Fourier transform, preserving Johnson-Lindenstrauss guarantees while cutting memory/compute cost substantially.

Experiments span two backbones (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B) and four diverse benchmarks (MMLU, ScienceQA, GSM8K, HumanEval), with consistent accuracy gains over strong baselines (MaxLoss, MaxGrad, RHO-Loss, GREATS) as well as throughput improvements over full-dataset training.

Reasonably thorough ablations (Table 4) isolate the contribution of the nuclear-norm and diversity-distance components, and sensitivity analyses for the projection dimensions d1/d2, buffer size M, and trade-off factor α are provided with quantified memory/time overhead (Figures 5-7), supporting the claim of negligible extra cost for these specific components.
The paper includes a reasonably transparent limitations section (SVD cost caveat) and detailed appendix with hyperparameters, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central theoretical argument connecting nuclear norm to optimization utility (Section 3.1) is qualitative rather than rigorous: the claim that ∆(x;θt) is 'less sensitive to scale' than δL is asserted without a formal bound, and the conclusion that nuclear norm, Frobenius norm, and loss reduction 'grow in tandem' rests on this informal reasoning rather than a proven inequality.

The most computationally concerning step of the method -- computing the nuclear norm via SVD of an N x V logits matrix for every candidate sample in every batch -- is not clearly benchmarked. The paper's overhead analysis (Figures 5-6) only accounts for the projection matrices used for inter-sample diversity, not the SVD cost itself, which could be substantial for large vocabularies (30k-150k) and long sequences, yet the throughput numbers in Table 3 supposedly already include this; more transparency on where this cost appears is needed.

The data selection ratios (Table 5) vary considerably and somewhat arbitrarily across dataset/backbone combinations (12.5%-50%), and there is no ablation showing how sensitive results are to this hyperparameter beyond a single MMLU/Llama-3.1-8B sweep (Figure 4); this raises reproducibility concerns since performance may be highly tuned to these specific ratios.

The batch size used throughout is quite small (B=8), meaning the 'online batch selection' setting operates over a very limited candidate pool per step; it is unclear how the method scales to more realistic large-batch training regimes common in LLM fine-tuning, and no experiments address this.

Only LoRA (rank=8) fine-tuning is evaluated; it is unclear whether the nuclear-norm-based scoring and gains generalize to full-parameter fine-tuning, which is a common and arguably more impactful SFT setting.

Baseline fairness is somewhat questionable: for RHO-Loss the paper substitutes a suboptimal reference model (Llama-2-13B rather than Llama-3.1-70B) for computational reasons, which the authors acknowledge but which may understate this baseline's true performance and bias the comparison in UDS's favor.

Only 4 random seeds are used for benchmark evaluation, which is a relatively small number given known variance in LLM fine-tuning and evaluation, especially for smaller benchmarks like HumanEval (164 examples).

The paper does not compare against simpler diversity-only baselines (e.g., entropy of the predictive distribution, or basic embedding-based deduplication) that could serve as more direct ablations of whether the specific nuclear-norm construction is necessary versus simpler alternatives already in the diversity/uncertainty literature the paper cites (e.g., Qiu & Miikkulainen, 2024).

strengths: The paper clearly articulates three desiderata (D1-D3) for online batch selection and systematically differentiates UDS from prior work (MaxLoss, MaxGrad, RHO-Loss, GREATS) in Table 1, giving a clear conceptual framing for the contribution.

The method is computationally elegant: it derives both a utility/intra-sample-diversity signal (nuclear norm of logits) and an inter-sample diversity signal (low-dimensional bilinear random projection with a memory buffer) purely from forward-pass quantities, avoiding backpropagation-heavy scoring or external reference models/validation sets used by baselines like RHO-Loss and GREATS.

The bilinear SRFT-style projection is theoretically grounded (Theorem 3.2, Appendix C.3) and reduces both storage and computational complexity relative to a naive full projection, and the algebraic reduction to a standard SRFT is a nice technical contribution.

The experimental evaluation is extensive: results across two backbones (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B), four datasets/tasks, ablations on both scoring components, sensitivity analyses on buffer size/projection dimensions/trade-off factor, and appendix studies covering full fine-tuning, larger batch sizes, instruction-tuned models, long-context (MATH), OOD generalization (MATH500/AMC23), and comparison with an offline baseline (FisherSFT) — this breadth strengthens confidence in the general applicability of the method.
UDS shows consistent accuracy improvements over baselines while maintaining higher training throughput than full-dataset SFT in most settings, directly supporting the paper's efficiency claims.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification connecting nuclear norm to optimization utility (Section 3.1) relies on a first-order Taylor expansion combined with an informal claim that the gradient term ∆(x;θ) is 'less sensitive to scale' than the logits norm; this argument is heuristic rather than rigorous, and the paper's own empirical support (Figure 2) is drawn from a single model/dataset combination (Qwen-2.5-7B on MMLU) with visibly noisy/variable correlation in early training, which is thin evidence for a core mechanistic claim underlying the entire method.

Similarly, the claim that nuclear norm captures intra-sample diversity relies on bound-achieving extreme cases (rank-1 vs. full-rank with equal singular values) that rarely occur in practice; the paper does not analyze how well this reasoning holds for typical intermediate-rank matrices actually encountered during training, again relying on a single correlation plot (Figure 3) from one setting.

The method's practical deployment requires per-dataset/per-backbone tuning of both the data selection fraction (Table 5) and the trade-off factor α (Table 6, with an inverted-U-shaped sensitivity), which is not obviously obtainable without some form of held-out validation signal — this appears to be in tension with desideratum D2 (no external resources/validation set), since choosing these hyperparameters well in a new setting without a validation set is unclear and not addressed.

Nuclear norm computation requires an SVD of the N×V logits matrix; while the authors mention this could be costly for long sequences/large vocabularies (acknowledged as a limitation and explored via randomized SVD with degraded performance), the actual wall-clock overhead of exact SVD for the vocab sizes used (e.g., Qwen/Llama vocab ~150K) is not clearly reported, raising questions about how the efficiency claims scale to even larger models or longer contexts.

Main experiments use LoRA (rank=8) rather than full fine-tuning as the primary setting, with full fine-tuning relegated to a single appendix table on one dataset/model combination; this limits confidence that conclusions transfer robustly to full-parameter SFT, which is a common practical regime.

The paper's central empirical claims of 'consistent' improvement, while generally true, are sometimes accompanied by relatively small margins in some benchmarks (e.g., ScienceQA, HumanEval) where confidence intervals of UDS and the strongest baseline (GREATS) are close, and no statistical significance testing (e.g., paired t-test) is reported beyond means and standard deviations.
The abstract states 'Code is available at' with no actual link provided in the manuscript text, which is a reproducibility concern if the repository is not clearly accessible to reviewers/readers.

strengths: Well-motivated framework: the paper articulates three clear desiderata (utility+diversity awareness, no external resources, training-time reduction) and systematically shows how prior methods fail to satisfy all three (Table 1), providing a clean conceptual contribution.

Technically interesting core idea: using the nuclear norm of the logits matrix as a unified score that captures both optimization utility (via first-order Taylor argument linking logits perturbation to loss reduction) and intra-sample diversity (via the Frobenius/nuclear norm bound in Lemma 3.1), with empirical support (Figures 2 and 3 show strong Spearman correlations across training).

The bilinear/Kronecker random projection (Theorem 3.2) is a nice practical solution to the storage blow-up problem of naive JL projection on logits matrices, with a rigorous reduction to an SRFT and JL guarantee, reducing complexity from O(NVd) to O((N+V)d log(NV)).

Extensive empirical validation: results span four benchmarks and two backbones, with additional appendix experiments covering larger batch sizes, full fine-tuning, instruction-tuned models, long-context (MATH) reasoning, OOD generalization (MATH500/AMC23), and comparison against an offline selection baseline (FisherSFT) — this breadth substantially strengthens the credibility of the claims.

Thorough ablations isolating the two score components (Table 4) and additional studies on buffer update policy, distance aggregation, and random matrix construction (Tables 7–9), plus sensitivity analysis on hyperparameters (d1, d2, M, α) with negligible extra memory/compute overhead reported.

UDS achieves both higher accuracy and higher training throughput than full-dataset training and existing online batch selection baselines (MaxLoss, MaxGrad, RHO-Loss, GREATS) across essentially all tested settings, addressing a genuine practical need (no reference model or validation set).
weaknesses: The link between nuclear norm and 'higher intra-sample diversity' relies on degenerate boundary cases of Lemma 3.1 (exact rank-1 vs. exact full-rank-equal-singular-value regimes); the argument for intermediate, realistic logits matrices is more heuristic/intuitive than rigorously established, a limitation the authors partially acknowledge.

The optimal data-selection ratio and trade-off factor α are highly dataset- and backbone-specific (Tables 5 and 6), requiring per-task tuning via sensitivity sweeps; no principled or automatic method for setting these is provided, which limits out-of-the-box practicality.

Most main experiments use LoRA (rank=8) rather than full fine-tuning, and although Table 11 includes one full-FT setting, it is limited to a single model/config, leaving open how well the nuclear-norm-based scoring generalizes across different fine-tuning paradigms and much larger candidate batch sizes than B=8.

Baseline tuning fidelity is somewhat uncertain (e.g., GREATS validation set size fixed at 5, RHO-Loss uses a smaller-than-ideal reference model for Llama-3.1-8B due to compute constraints), which could understate baseline performance and make relative gains look larger than they would be with fully tuned baselines.

The theoretical optimization-utility argument (Eq. 5–8) is a first-order Taylor approximation under simplified SGD assumptions (with an Adam extension provided only heuristically in the appendix); no formal bound on approximation error or discussion of when the linearization breaks down (e.g., large learning rates, non-trivial curvature) is given.
